entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 7 So 7:1-13 . 1. thy feet-- rather, "thy goings" ( Psa 17:5 ). Evident allusion to Is 52:7 : "How beautiful ... are the feet of him ... that publisheth peace" (Shulamite, So 6:13 ). shoes-- Sandals are richly jewelled in the East ( Lu 15:22 ; Ep 6:15 ). She is evidently "on the mountains," whither she was wafted ( So 6:12 ), above the daughters of Jerusalem, who therefore portray her feet first. daughter-- of God the Father, with whom Jesus Christ is one ( Mt 5:9 ), "children of (the) God" (of peace), equivalent to Shulamite ( Psa 45:10-15 ; 2Co 6:18 ), as well as bride of Jesus Christ. prince's-- therefore princely herself, freely giving the word of life to others, not sparing her "feet," as in So 5:3 ; Ex 12:11 . To act on the offensive is defensive to ourselves. joints-- rather, "the rounding"; the full graceful curve of the hips in the female figure; like the rounding of a necklace (as the Hebrew for "jewels" means). Compare with the English Version, Ep 4:13-16 ; Col 2:19 . Or, applying it to the girdle binding together the robes round the hips ( Ep 6:14 ). cunning workman-- ( Psa 139:14-16 ; Ep 2:10 , 22; 5:29, 30, 32).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8282"/><div sID="gen13119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8282"/><hi type="bold">2. navel--</hi>rather, "girdle-clasp," called from the part of the person underneath. The "shoes" (<reference osisRef="Song.7.1">So 7:1</reference>) prove that dress is throughout presupposed on all parts where it is usually worn. She is "a bride adorned for her husband"; the "uncomely parts," being most adorned (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.23">1Co 12:23</reference>). The girdle-clasp was adorned with red rubies resembling the "round goblet" (crater or mixer) of spice-mixed wine (not "liquor," <reference osisRef="Song.8.2">So 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">Is 5:22</reference>). The wine of the "New Testament in His blood" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.20">Lu 22:20</reference>). The spiritual exhilaration by it was mistaken for that caused by new wine (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.13-Acts.2.17">Ac 2:13-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.18">Ep 5:18</reference>).<div eID="gen13119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">belly--</hi>that is, the vesture on it. As in <reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Psa 45:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">14</reference>, gold and needlework compose the bride's attire, so golden-colored "wheat" and white "lilies" here. The ripe grain, in token of harvest joy, used to be decorated with lilies; so the accumulated spiritual food (<reference osisRef="John.6.35">Joh 6:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.24">12:24</reference>), free from chaff, not fenced with thorns, but made attractive by lilies ("believers," <reference osisRef="Song.2.2">So 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.46">Ac 2:46</reference>, 47; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.13">5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.14">14</reference>, in common partaking of it). Associated with the exhilarating wine cup (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.17">Zec 9:17</reference>), as here. <div eID="gen13120" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8284"/><div sID="gen13123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8284"/><hi type="bold">4. tower of ivory--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Song.4.4">So 4:4</reference>, Jesus Christ saith, "a tower of David builded for an armory." Strength and conquest are the main thought in His description; here, beauty and polished whiteness; contrast <reference osisRef="Song.1.5">So 1:5</reference>.<div eID="gen13123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fishpools--</hi>seen by Burckhardt, clear (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Re 22:1</reference>), deep, quiet, and full (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen13124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Heshbon--</hi>east of Jordan, residence of the Amorite king, Sihon (<reference osisRef="Num.21.25">Nu 21:25</reference>, &c.), afterwards held by Gad.<div eID="gen13125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bath-rabbim--</hi>"daughter of a multitude"; a crowded thoroughfare. Her eyes (<reference osisRef="Song.4.1">So 4:1</reference>) are called by Jesus Christ, "doves' eyes," waiting on Him. But here, looked on by the daughters or Jerusalem, they are compared to a placid lake. She is calm even amidst the crowd (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.2">Pr 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.33">Joh 16:33</reference>).<div eID="gen13126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nose--</hi>or, face.<div eID="gen13127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tower of Lebanon--</hi>a border-fortress, watching the hostile Damascus. Towards Jesus Christ her face was full of holy shame (see on <reference osisRef="Song.4.1">So 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.4.3">So 4:3</reference>); towards spiritual foes, like a watchtower (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Ha 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.13.37">Mr 13:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.13">Ac 4:13</reference>), elevated, so that she looks not up from earth to heaven, but down from heaven to earth. If we retain "nose," discernment of spiritual fragrance is meant. <div eID="gen13128" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8285"/><div sID="gen13129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8285"/><hi type="bold">5. upon thee--</hi>the headdress "upon" her.<div eID="gen13129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Carmel--</hi>signifying a well-cultivated field (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.2">Is 35:2</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Song.5.15">So 5:15</reference> He is compared to majestic Lebanon; she here, to fruitful Carmel. Her headdress, or crown (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.4">1Pe 5:4</reference>). Also the souls won by her (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.19">1Th 2:19</reference>, 20), a token of her fruitfulness.<div eID="gen13130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13131" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purple--</hi>royalty (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Re 1:6</reference>). As applied to hair, it expresses the glossy splendor of black hair (literally, "pendulous hair") so much admired in the East (<reference osisRef="Song.4.1">So 4:1</reference>). While the King compares her hair to the flowering hair of goats (the token of her subjection), the daughters of Jerusalem compare it to royal purple.<div eID="gen13131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">galleries--</hi>(so <reference osisRef="Song.1.17">So 1:17</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Re 21:3</reference>). But Maurer translates here, "flowing ringlets"; with these, as with "thongs" (so Lee, from the Arabic translates it) "the King is held" bound (<reference osisRef="Song.6.5">So 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.25">Pr 6:25</reference>). Her purple crowns of martyrdom especially captivated the King, appearing from His galleries (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.55">Ac 7:55</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.56">56</reference>). As Samson's strength was in his locks (<reference osisRef="Judg.16.17">Jud 16:17</reference>). Here first the daughters see the King themselves. <div eID="gen13132" type="x-p"/>

Here first the daughters see the King themselves.

But here she prepares for Him all kinds of fruit old and new; also, she anticipates, in going forth to seek them, communion with Him in "loves." "Early" implies immediate earnestness. "The villages" imply distance from Jerusalem. At Stephen's death the disciples were scattered from it through Judea and Samaria, preaching the word (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.4-Acts.8.25">Ac 8:4-25</reference>).
